Reference: Saez (2010)

Model Setting

The paper asks whether taxpayers bunch at convex kink points of the US income tax and transfer schedule, as the standard static labor supply model predicts, and shows how the amount of bunching can be turned into an estimate of the compensated elasticity of reported income with respect to the net-of-tax rate. In the standard model with convex preferences that are smoothly distributed in the population, a jump in the marginal tax rate at income level z∗z^*z∗ makes everyone whose income would have fallen in a small segment just above z∗z^*z∗ locate exactly at z∗z^*z∗, and the mass of this spike is proportional to the elasticity times the jump in the log net-of-tax rate. The paper derives this result for small kinks, extends it to large kinks with a quasi-linear iso-elastic utility and a trapezoid approximation of the counterfactual density, and proposes an excess-mass estimator based on three income bands around the kink, with delta-method and bootstrap standard errors. It is the paper that introduced the modern bunching estimator.

The data are the IRS Individual Public Use Tax Files, stratified random cross sections of 80,000 to 200,000 returns per year available quasi-annually from 1960 to 2004, used with sampling weights. Administrative data locate taxpayers exactly on the schedule and have almost no measurement error. There are three main findings. First, there is clear bunching at the first kink of the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC), where the credit reaches its maximum, with an implied elasticity of about 0.25 in the full sample, but the bunching comes entirely from filers with self-employment income (elasticity around one), while wage earners show none (a precisely estimated zero); bunching grows over time. There is no bunching at the second EITC kink and no hole at the concave kink where the credit ends. Second, there is bunching at the threshold of the first income tax bracket, where tax liability starts, especially in the stable 1960s, with elasticities around 0.2, partly driven by itemized deductions. Third, there is no bunching at any higher kink of the income tax, even large and stable ones, and even among the self-employed. A fixed-cost model of misreporting informal self-employment income explains the EITC facts better than the standard model.

Standard Model and Small Kink

Individuals have utility u(c,z)u(c,z)u(c,z) increasing in after-tax income ccc and decreasing in before-tax income zzz, which requires effort. Heterogeneity in preferences or ability is captured by heterogeneity in uuu. Under a linear tax with constant marginal rate ttt, incomes are distributed with a smooth density h(z)h(z)h(z). Introduce a small kink at z∗z^*z∗ by raising the marginal rate from ttt to t+dtt+dtt+dt above z∗z^*z∗. The indifference-curve argument works as follows. Individual L, who chose z∗z^*z∗ before the reform, is unaffected: the indifference curve stays tangent to the lower segment of slope 1−t1-t1−t. Individual H is the highest pre-reform earner who now bunches: before the reform H chose z∗+dz∗z^*+dz^*z∗+dz∗ with an indifference curve tangent to the line of slope 1−t1-t1−t, and after the reform the indifference curve through z∗z^*z∗ is exactly tangent to the upper segment of slope 1−t−dt1-t-dt1−t−dt. Everyone between L and H moves to the kink. By definition of the compensated elasticity eee of earnings with respect to one minus the tax rate:

dz∗z∗=edt1−t(1)\frac{dz^*}{z^*}=e\frac{dt}{1-t} \tag{1}z∗dz∗​=e1−tdt​(1)

Bunching is therefore proportional to the elasticity and to the net-of-tax ratio dt/(1−t)dt/(1-t)dt/(1−t): with no behavioral response there is no bunching, and a rise in the marginal rate from 0 to 10 percent produces the same bunching as a rise from 90 to 91 percent. For large jumps, eee would mix compensated and uncompensated elasticities because of income effects.

Estimating Excess Bunching

For an empirical distribution h(z)h(z)h(z), the paper defines a bandwidth δ\deltaδ, an income band (z∗−δ,z∗+δ)(z^*-\delta,z^*+\delta)(z∗−δ,z∗+δ) around the kink and two surrounding bands (z∗−2δ,z∗−δ)(z^*-2\delta,z^*-\delta)(z∗−2δ,z∗−δ) and (z∗+δ,z∗+2δ)(z^*+\delta,z^*+2\delta)(z∗+δ,z∗+2δ). Excess bunching is the population in the middle band minus the populations in the two side bands:

B=∫z∗−δz∗+δh(z)dz−∫z∗−2δz∗−δh(z)dz−∫z∗+δz∗+2δh(z)dz(16)B=\int_{z^*-\delta}^{z^*+\delta}h(z)dz-\int_{z^*-2\delta}^{z^*-\delta}h(z)dz-\int_{z^*+\delta}^{z^*+2\delta}h(z)dz \tag{16}B=∫z∗−δz∗+δ​h(z)dz−∫z∗−2δz∗−δ​h(z)dz−∫z∗+δz∗+2δ​h(z)dz(16)

Since the middle band is twice as wide as each side band, this subtracts a linear counterfactual density. Taxpayers cannot control incomes perfectly (year-end bonuses, risky asset returns, difficulty in forecasting taxable income), may not know where kinks are, and data may contain measurement error, so they cluster around the kink rather than bunch exactly at it (Saez (1999) formalizes this with uncertain outcomes). These optimization frictions make the choice of δ\deltaδ matter. If δ\deltaδ is too small, the side bands contain clustered bunchers and excess bunching is underestimated. If δ\deltaδ is too large, the curvature of the counterfactual density h0(z)h_0(z)h0​(z) biases the estimate: a concave h0h_0h0​ makes BBB positive even without any response, and a convex h0h_0h0​ biases it downward (the paper states the reverse). A Taylor-expansion correction for curvature is possible with larger samples (Chetty et al. (2009) fit the density nonparametrically outside the bunching segment). The paper chooses δ\deltaδ graphically so that the full hump lies inside (z∗−δ,z∗+δ)(z^*-\delta,z^*+\delta)(z∗−δ,z∗+δ).

The side densities are the population shares of the side bands divided by δ\deltaδ. Denote by H^−∗,H^∗,H^+∗\hat{H}^*_-,\hat{H}^*,\hat{H}^*_+H^−∗​,H^∗,H^+∗​ the estimated numbers of individuals in the lower, middle and upper bands, obtained by simultaneously regressing dummies for membership in each band on a constant in the sample of individuals in any of the three bands. Then:

h^(z∗)+=H^+∗δ,h^(z∗)−=H^−∗δ,B^=H^∗−(H^+∗+H^−∗)(17)\hat{h}(z^*)_+=\frac{\hat{H}^*_+}{\delta},\qquad\hat{h}(z^*)_-=\frac{\hat{H}^*_-}{\delta},\qquad\hat{B}=\hat{H}^*-\left(\hat{H}^*_++\hat{H}^*_-\right) \tag{17}h^(z∗)+​=δH^+∗​​,h^(z∗)−​=δH^−∗​​,B^=H^∗−(H^+∗​+H^−∗​)(17)

and these are plugged into the bunching formula to obtain e^\hat{e}e^. Standard errors come from the delta method applied to the joint estimates of the three band shares, or from a bootstrap that draws NNN earnings distributions from the empirical distribution and re-estimates eee in each draw. With large samples the two give very similar standard errors. Graphical detection uses histograms with small bins to look for spikes, and kernel densities to detect humps. Kinks created by state taxes and other transfers vary geographically and use other income definitions, so the bunching they generate is smoothed out in the aggregate.

The EITC Schedule

The EITC depends on family earnings (wages and salaries plus self-employment income) and the number of qualifying children. It first rises linearly with earnings (phase-in), is flat at its maximum (plateau) and is then phased out linearly. Writing T′(z)T'(z)T′(z) for the marginal tax rate created by the credit, the 1995 to 2008 schedule in 2008 dollars for one child is:

T′(z)={−0.340<z<8,58008,580<z<15,7400.1615,740<z<33,9950z>33,995(18)T'(z)=\begin{cases}-0.34 & 0<z<8{,}580\\ 0 & 8{,}580<z<15{,}740\\ 0.16 & 15{,}740<z<33{,}995\\ 0 & z>33{,}995\end{cases} \tag{18}T′(z)=⎩⎨⎧​−0.3400.160​0<z<8,5808,580<z<15,74015,740<z<33,995z>33,995​(18)

For two or more children the phase-in rate is 40 percent up to 12,060 dollars, the plateau ends at 15,740 dollars and the phase-out rate is 21 percent up to 38,646 dollars. Maximum credits are 2,917 and 4,824 dollars. The first kink is therefore a convex kink from t0=−0.34t_0=-0.34t0​=−0.34 (or −0.40-0.40−0.40) to t1=0t_1=0t1​=0, the second a convex kink from 0 to 16 (or 21) percent, and the third a concave kink. From 1988 to 1993 the credit was small and did not depend on the number of children, with a phase-in rate of 14 percent up to 11,416 dollars, a plateau to 18,002 dollars and a 10 percent phase-out to 33,985 dollars, and in 1991 to 1993 phase-in rates rose gradually to about 17 to 20 percent. The EITC was expanded after the Tax Reform Act of 1986 and very substantially in 1993 to 1995, and has been stable since. Earnings are indexed to 2008 using the IRS inflation parameters so that kinks are aligned across years.

EITC Evidence

Histograms with 500-dollar bins pooling 1995 to 2004 (57,692 observations representing 116 million returns with one child, and 67,038 representing 115 million with two or more) show that the density is maximal exactly at the first kink in both groups. Because the first kink is at different earnings levels for the two groups, the clustering must be a behavioral response. There is no clustering at the second kink and no gap at the end of the phase-out. Splitting by self-employment status, the self-employed (nonzero self-employment income, 16.1 and about 20 percent of the weighted population, 32 and 40 percent of the sample) show a huge spike exactly at the first kink, while pure wage earners show none. The self-employed with one child bunch more than those with two or more children, although their kink is smaller. Bunching among the self-employed grows sharply from 1995 to 1999 to 2000 to 2004, which the paper attributes to slow diffusion of knowledge about how to game the EITC with self-employment income, rather than to adjustment costs, since wage earners never develop bunching.

  • First kink, 1995 to 2004 (δ\deltaδ of 1,500 dollars): elasticities are 0.213 (0.033) for all filers with one child and 0.152 (0.020) with two or more children; 1.101 (0.092) and 0.755 (0.054) for the self-employed; and 0.025 (0.036) and 0.003 (0.022) for wage earners. Bootstrap standard errors are almost identical (for example 0.107 instead of 0.092).

  • Second and third kinks: all estimates are small, insignificant and precisely estimated, between −0.032-0.032−0.032 and 0.016.

  • Bandwidth: with δ\deltaδ of 2,000 dollars the first-kink estimates rise to 0.320, 0.186, 1.639 and 0.954 for the first four columns; with 1,000 dollars they fall to 0.165, 0.107, 0.751 and 0.379. The baseline is conservative because the side bands are already affected by clustering, and the differences across bandwidths are significant.

  • Dynamics: from 1995 to 1999 to 2000 to 2004, self-employed elasticities rise from 0.703 to 1.424 (one child) and from 0.526 to 0.937 (two or more), while wage earners stay near zero (−0.002-0.002−0.002 to 0.056).

  • Small EITC, 1988 to 1993: first-kink elasticities are 0.092 for all filers, 0.207 for the self-employed and 0.071 for wage earners; the self-employed estimate is insignificant in 1988 to 1990 (0.165, standard error 0.139, subsidy rate 14 percent) and significant in 1991 to 1993 (0.229, standard error 0.088, rates of 17 to 19 percent), when a spike develops exactly at the kink.

A Model of Tax Reporting

The standard model cannot explain why the self-employed bunch only at the first kink and only when the subsidy rate exceeds about 15 percent. Self-employment income bears the Social Security and Medicare payroll tax of 15.3 percent, collected on the income tax return, so the first EITC kink maximizes the net transfer from the government exactly when the subsidy rate exceeds 15.3 percent. Each individual has formal earnings w≥0w\geq0w≥0, third-party reported and impossible to misreport, and informal earnings y≥0y\geq0y≥0, which can be misreported. Neither responds to taxes on the intensive margin and both are smoothly distributed. With reported informal income y^\hat{y}y^​, disposable income is:

c=w+y−T(w+y^)(19)c=w+y-T(w+\hat{y}) \tag{19}c=w+y−T(w+y^​)(19)

Preferences are linear with fixed costs instead of convex: an administrative cost qAq_AqA​ of reporting y^>0\hat{y}>0y^​>0 (record keeping, extra schedules, computing the liability), and a moral cost qMq_MqM​ paid whenever y^≠y\hat{y}\neq yy^​=y (the psychological cost of cheating or of an audit). Reports y^<0\hat{y}<0y^​<0 are ruled out because they would trigger an audit, consistent with the absence of bunching among those reporting losses. The individual chooses y^\hat{y}y^​ to maximize:

w+y−T(w+y^)−qA1(y^>0)−qM1(y^≠y)(20)w+y-T(w+\hat{y})-q_A\mathbf{1}(\hat{y}>0)-q_M\mathbf{1}(\hat{y}\neq y) \tag{20}w+y−T(w+y^​)−qA​1(y^​>0)−qM​1(y^​=y)(20)

Assume −T(z)-T(z)−T(z) is single peaked with unique maximizer z∗z^*z∗: the first EITC kink if the subsidy rate exceeds the payroll tax rate, and z∗=0z^*=0z∗=0 otherwise. The costs (qA,qM)(q_A,q_M)(qA​,qM​) are smoothly distributed.

Proposition 1. (i) The optimal report takes only three values: truthful reporting y^=y\hat{y}=yy^​=y, complete evasion y^=0\hat{y}=0y^​=0, or refund maximization y^=z∗−w\hat{y}=z^*-wy^​=z∗−w. (ii) If z∗>0z^*>0z∗>0, an atom of filers bunches at z∗z^*z∗. For (i), if z∗−w≥0z^*-w\geq0z∗−w≥0 and y^>0\hat{y}>0y^​>0 with y^≠y\hat{y}\neq yy^​=y, both fixed costs are already paid, so y^\hat{y}y^​ must do at least as well as z∗−wz^*-wz∗−w, which requires w+y^=z∗w+\hat{y}=z^*w+y^​=z∗ by uniqueness of the maximizer; if z∗−w<0z^*-w<0z∗−w<0, single-peakedness makes y^=0\hat{y}=0y^​=0 the best misreport. For (ii), the filer compares the three values:

Every filer with:

bunches at the kink. Both right-hand sides are positive whenever w≠z∗w\neq z^*w=z∗ and w+y≠z∗w+y\neq z^*w+y=z∗, so with smoothly distributed costs a positive measure of filers bunches. When the subsidy rate is below the payroll tax rate, filers are truthful or do not report informal income at all, as in compliance studies. Above it, bunchers are former non-reporters with a gain above qAq_AqA​ and former truthful reporters with a gain above qMq_MqM​. There is no bunching at the second kink, which does not maximize the net credit, and a convex cost of evasion would bring back convex preferences and bunching there. Bunching rises with the net credit −T(z∗)-T(z^*)−T(z∗), and its growth can be modeled as slow learning from others or from tax preparers. Since a marginal EITC increase induces reporting responses with a first-order fiscal cost but a second-order private gain, these responses are deadweight burden, proportional to the size of the response.

The Federal Income Tax

Taxable income is adjusted gross income (AGI) minus personal exemptions minus the larger of the standard deduction and itemized deductions. The paper compares it with taxable income recomputed with the standard deduction:

z=AGI−exemptions−max⁡(standard,itemized),zSD=AGI−exemptions−standard(23)z=\text{AGI}-\text{exemptions}-\max\left(\text{standard},\text{itemized}\right),\qquad z^{SD}=\text{AGI}-\text{exemptions}-\text{standard} \tag{23}z=AGI−exemptions−max(standard,itemized),zSD=AGI−exemptions−standard(23)

Before the Tax Reform Act of 1986 there were 15 to 25 brackets with small jumps, except at the first kink, the schedule was not indexed, and kinks moved with inflation (bracket creep), so the analysis uses 1960 to 1969 and only the first kink. From 1948 to 1963 exemptions were 600 dollars per person, the standard deduction was 10 percent of AGI up to 1,000 dollars and the first rate was 20 percent; in 1964 a more generous standard deduction was introduced and the first rate fell to 16 and then 14 percent; exemptions and standard deductions were raised annually from 1970. After 1986 the schedule is indexed, with kinks from 0 to 15 percent at zero taxable income and from 15 to 28 percent (54,350 dollars for married couples in 2008 dollars), 31 to 36 and 36 to 39.6 percent from 1993, and a 10 percent bottom bracket from 2002. With nonrefundable credits ddd, the first kink is not at zero but at:

z=dτ1(24)z=\frac{d}{\tau_1} \tag{24}z=τ1​d​(24)

where τ1\tau_1τ1​ is the first-bracket rate, so the child tax credit of 1998 moves the kink away from zero for most low-income filers with children. Because the elasticity is not defined at z∗=0z^*=0z∗=0, the base income z∗z^*z∗ in the bunching formula at the first kink is the average AGI of filers with taxable income in (−δ,δ)(-\delta,\delta)(−δ,δ). Dependents are excluded.

Federal Income Tax Evidence

In 1960 to 1969 (years 1960, 1962, 1964 and 1966 to 1969), taxable income densities of married joint filers and of other filers peak just at the first kink, and there is no missing mass below it because withholding makes low earners file for refunds. Bunching is much weaker for zSDz^{SD}zSD, especially for married filers, so a large part comes from itemized deductions (for example charitable contributions), though some AGI response remains, especially for singles. Bunching falls after the 1964 and 1970 reforms, again showing that filers learn slowly. In 1988 to 2002 bunching at zero taxable income is present but weaker, absent at the 15 to 28 percent kink even for the self-employed or capital gains realizers, and it disappears for filers with children after 1998, when the child tax credit removes the kink at zero.

  • First kink: 0.209 (0.018) for all filers in 1960 to 1969 (δ\deltaδ of 1,500 dollars), with 0.170 for married and 0.263 for single filers; 0.162 (0.012) in 1988 to 2002 (δ\deltaδ of 2,000 dollars), with 0.113 and 0.191.

  • Bandwidth: in 1988 to 2002 the all-filer estimate is 0.096 with δ\deltaδ of 1,500 dollars and 0.228 with 2,500 dollars, still significant.

  • Dynamics: 0.217 in 1960 to 1963, 0.204 in 1964 to 1969 and 0.094 in 1970 to 1972; for singles the drop is from 0.352 to 0.062.

  • Higher kinks, 1988 to 2004: 0.005 (0.005) at the 15 to 28 percent kink (0.022 for the self-employed), 0.031 at 31 to 36 percent and 0.006 at 36 to 39.6 percent, all zero and precisely estimated.

The absence of bunching at higher kinks is inconsistent with the static model underlying the taxable income elasticity literature if those elasticities are substantial. Possible explanations are stochastic incomes at the top, dynamic career concerns that make the local Frisch elasticity small, larger elasticities or more flexibility at the bottom, and the greater salience of the point where tax liability starts. The estimator can be applied to other convex kinks, such as the Social Security earnings test, 401(k) employer matches and retirement incentives.

This is the assumed quasi-linear, iso-elastic utility. Consumption ccc (after-tax income) enters linearly, and the disutility of earning zzz is a power function scaled by ability nnn. The parameter e>0e>0e>0 is the earnings elasticity; nnn is the individual's type, distributed with density f(n)f(n)f(n) and CDF F(n)F(n)F(n) in a population of mass one.

Quasi-linearity removes income effects: the virtual income RRR of a linear budget c=(1−t)z+Rc=(1-t)z+Rc=(1−t)z+R does not affect the choice of zzz, so compensated and uncompensated elasticities coincide and bunching at large kinks can be interpreted without separating the two. Iso-elasticity makes the elasticity constant: the marginal disutility is (z/n)1/e(z/n)^{1/e}(z/n)1/e, so the log of optimal earnings is linear in the log of the net-of-tax rate with slope eee (equation (5)). The scaling by nnn is chosen so that nnn equals earnings at a zero tax rate:

What this rules out: heterogeneous elasticities (handled separately by equations (2) and (3)), income effects, and optimization frictions. Its payoff is that the whole earnings distribution under any linear tax is a rescaling of the ability distribution, which gives the closed forms in equations (6) to (10).

This is the empirical definition of excess bunching from three income bands of width δ\deltaδ, 2δ2\delta2δ and δ\deltaδ: the population in the middle band (z∗−δ,z∗+δ)(z^*-\delta,z^*+\delta)(z∗−δ,z∗+δ) minus the populations in the lower band (z∗−2δ,z∗−δ)(z^*-2\delta,z^*-\delta)(z∗−2δ,z∗−δ) and the upper band (z∗+δ,z∗+2δ)(z^*+\delta,z^*+2\delta)(z∗+δ,z∗+2δ). Here h(z)h(z)h(z) is the observed density with the kink, and δ\deltaδ is a bandwidth in dollars chosen so that the hump of clustered bunchers falls inside the middle band.

Why it measures BBB: suppose the observed density equals h(z∗)−h(z^*)_-h(z∗)−​ on the left and h(z∗)+h(z^*)_+h(z∗)+​ on the right (locally flat on each side) plus an atom BBB near z∗z^*z∗. Then the middle band contains δh(z∗)−+δh(z∗)++B\delta h(z^*)_-+\delta h(z^*)_++Bδh(z∗)−​+δh(z∗)+​+B and the side bands contain δh(z∗)−\delta h(z^*)_-δh(z∗)−​ and δh(z∗)+\delta h(z^*)_+δh(z∗)+​, so the difference is exactly BBB, even though the density jumps at the kink. More generally, if hhh is linear on each band, the middle band has twice the width of each side band and the subtraction removes it.

Curvature bias: with no behavioral response and a smooth counterfactual h0(z)=a+b(z−z∗)+c(z−z∗)2h_0(z)=a+b(z-z^*)+c(z-z^*)^2h0​(z)=a+b(z−z∗)+c(z−z∗)2,

∫z∗−δz∗+δh0dz−∫z∗−2δz∗−δh0dz−∫z∗+δz∗+2δh0dz=(2aδ+2cδ33)−(2aδ+14cδ33)=−4cδ3.\int_{z^*-\delta}^{z^*+\delta}h_0dz-\int_{z^*-2\delta}^{z^*-\delta}h_0dz-\int_{z^*+\delta}^{z^*+2\delta}h_0dz=\left(2a\delta+\frac{2c\delta^3}{3}\right)-\left(2a\delta+\frac{14c\delta^3}{3}\right)=-4c\delta^3 .∫z∗−δz∗+δ​h0​dz−∫z∗−2δz∗−δ​h0​dz−∫z∗+δz∗+2δ​h0​dz=(2aδ+32cδ3​)−(2aδ+314cδ3​)=−4cδ3.

So a convex h0h_0h0​ (c>0c>0c>0) makes the formula negative without any response, i.e. biases excess bunching downward, and a concave h0h_0h0​ biases it upward; the bias grows with δ3\delta^3δ3. The note (following the paper, p. 187 and the Figure 2 notes) states the opposite, that a convex h0h_0h0​ makes BBB positive and leads to overestimation; that prose claim is reversed. The equation itself is correct. The choice of δ\deltaδ thus trades off missing diffuse bunchers (small δ\deltaδ) against curvature bias (large δ\deltaδ). The estimate feeds equation (17) and then equation (14).

This is the marginal tax rate T′(z)T'(z)T′(z) generated by the EITC for a filer with one child, 1995 to 2008, in 2008 dollars, where zzz is family earnings. A negative marginal rate is a subsidy: in the phase-in region each extra dollar earned raises the credit by 34 cents. On the plateau the credit is constant at its maximum, so the marginal rate is zero. In the phase-out region the credit falls by 16 cents per dollar, a positive marginal rate. Beyond the end of the phase-out the EITC no longer affects the marginal rate. Consistency checks:

0.34×8,580≈2,917,0.16×(33,995−15,740)≈2,921,0.34\times8{,}580\approx2{,}917,\qquad0.16\times(33{,}995-15{,}740)\approx2{,}921 ,0.34×8,580≈2,917,0.16×(33,995−15,740)≈2,921,

so the credit built up in the phase-in is (up to rounding) fully withdrawn in the phase-out. The schedule produces three kinks: at 8,580 the rate jumps from t0=−0.34t_0=-0.34t0​=−0.34 to t1=0t_1=0t1​=0 (convex; the log net-of-tax rate falls by ln⁡1.34≈0.29\ln1.34\approx0.29ln1.34≈0.29), at 15,740 from 0 to 0.16 (convex, ln⁡(1/0.84)≈0.17\ln(1/0.84)\approx0.17ln(1/0.84)≈0.17), and at 33,995 from 0.16 to 0 (concave, which should create a hole rather than a spike). These (t0,t1)(t_0,t_1)(t0​,t1​) pairs enter equation (14). The EITC schedule ignores the 15.3 percent payroll tax on self-employment income, which matters for equations (20) to (22).

This is the budget constraint of the reporting model. Each filer has formal earnings w≥0w\geq0w≥0 (wages, reported by third parties and impossible to misreport) and informal earnings y≥0y\geq0y≥0 (self-employment income, which can be misreported). True disposable income is total true income w+yw+yw+y minus the net tax T(⋅)T(\cdot)T(⋅) (taxes minus transfers, including the EITC and the payroll tax on self-employment income), which is levied on reported income w+y^w+\hat{y}w+y^​, not true income. Neither www nor yyy responds to taxes on the intensive margin: the only choice is the report y^\hat{y}y^​. Thus the model abstracts entirely from real labor supply and places all the behavioral response in reporting. Since w+yw+yw+y is fixed, maximizing ccc means minimizing T(w+y^)T(w+\hat{y})T(w+y^​); for example, with TTT minimized at z∗z^*z∗,

y^=z∗−w  ⇒  c=w+y−T(z∗),\hat{y}=z^*-w\;\Rightarrow\;c=w+y-T(z^*),y^​=z∗−w⇒c=w+y−T(z∗),

which is the bunching option in equation (21). Without the fixed costs of equation (20), every filer with w<z∗w<z^*w<z∗ would report z∗−wz^*-wz∗−w.

This is the filer's objective: disposable income from equation (19) minus two fixed costs. qAq_AqA​ is an administrative cost paid only if positive informal income is reported, y^>0\hat{y}>0y^​>0 (record keeping, schedules, computing the liability). qMq_MqM​ is a moral or audit-risk cost paid whenever the report differs from the truth, y^≠y\hat{y}\neq yy^​=y, whether by under- or over-reporting. Both are in dollars and are smoothly distributed in the population; reports y^<0\hat{y}<0y^​<0 are excluded because they would trigger an audit.

The preferences are linear in money and the costs are fixed rather than convex in the amount misreported. This is the key departure from the standard model: with fixed costs, once a filer misreports at all, the size of the misreport is free, so he goes all the way to the report that minimizes TTT. That is why the model produces bunching only at the global maximizer z∗z^*z∗ of −T(z)-T(z)−T(z) (the first EITC kink when the subsidy exceeds the payroll tax rate) and not at the second EITC kink, whereas a convex cost of evasion would generate bunching at every convex kink. The objective is analyzed in equations (21) and (22).

These are the two income concepts used for the federal income tax analysis. Taxable income zzz is adjusted gross income (AGI) minus personal exemptions minus the larger of the standard deduction and itemized deductions (all in dollars per return); this is the base on which the bracket rates apply, so the kinks of the schedule are located in zzz. The counterfactual zSDz^{SD}zSD recomputes taxable income as if every filer took the standard deduction. Since max⁡(standard,itemized)≥standard\max(\text{standard},\text{itemized})\geq\text{standard}max(standard,itemized)≥standard,

zSD−z=max⁡(0,itemized−standard)≥0,z^{SD}-z=\max\left(0,\text{itemized}-\text{standard}\right)\geq0 ,zSD−z=max(0,itemized−standard)≥0,

with equality for non-itemizers. The comparison is a decomposition device: if filers reach the first kink (zero taxable income) by adjusting itemized deductions such as charitable contributions, bunching appears in zzz but is smoothed out in zSDz^{SD}zSD; bunching that survives in zSDz^{SD}zSD must come from AGI (earnings or other income) responses. The paper finds much weaker bunching in zSDz^{SD}zSD, especially for married filers, so a large part of first-kink bunching operates through itemized deductions.
